country.evidence_source: [/page/0/Text/17] In the early 2000s, demographic statistics signaling a rapid decrease in fertility rates sounded the alarm for South Korean policymakers. These declining fertility rates were coupled with increased rates of women's employment and, as a result, an increase in the number of dual income households. In 2005, Korea's birth rate was at a historically low point, with 1.08 births per woman. Korean cultural background and traditions, with its strong male breadwinner ideology, has meant that many women have had to make a harsh tradeoff between work and a career on the one hand, and having a family and children on the other hand.
